title: Particulate Nature of Matter
subject: Science
objective: The particle model says that all matter is made of:
Extremely small particles with spaces between them
Matter consists of tiny particles; the spaces, motion and attraction between them explain how materials behave.
Grinding a piece of jaggery into a fine powder changes:
Only the size of each piece; every speck is still jaggery
Breaking or grinding is a physical change; the tiny grains remain the same substance.
A metal spoon keeps its shape no matter which container it is placed in, because:
Its particles are strongly held in fixed positions
In solids, strong interparticle attractions hold particles in fixed positions, giving a fixed shape and volume.
Honey poured into a jar slowly takes the jar's shape because:
Its particles stay close but can move past each other
Liquid particles are close together but not fixed, so liquids flow and take the shape of their container.
A syringe filled with air, its tip closed, can be pushed in a little. This shows that:
Gas particles have large spaces between them that can be squeezed smaller
Gases are compressible because their particles are far apart with large interparticle spaces.
An agarbatti lit in one corner soon smells across the whole room because:
Gas particles are in constant motion and spread through the air, mixing with it
Diffusion in gases is fast because their particles move freely and spread into all available space.
Sugar mixes faster in hot milk than in cold milk because:
At higher temperatures the particles move faster, so mixing and dissolving happen more quickly
Heating increases particle motion, which speeds up spreading and dissolving.
A spoonful of salt stirred into a pot of dal makes the whole pot taste salty because:
The dissolved salt particles spread uniformly among the particles of the liquid
Dal has no taste of its own
On dissolving, the particles of the solute spread evenly throughout the liquid, so every part tastes the same.
A wet handkerchief dries faster on a sunny railing than in a closed room because:
Warmth increases the motion of water particles, so evaporation is faster
Evaporation speeds up when heating increases particle motion and moving air carries the vapour away.
On a hot afternoon, solid ghee in a jar turns liquid. This change is:
Melting is a physical change: the particles gain energy and move more freely, but no new substance forms.
subjective: State four main ideas of the particle model of matter.

Any four: matter is made of tiny particles; there are spaces between the particles; particles are in constant motion; particles attract one another; the arrangement and motion of particles differ in solids, liquids and gases; heating increases particle motion while cooling decreases it.
Half mark per correct idea, up to 2 marks.
Ice, water and steam are the same substance. Using the particle model, explain why they behave so differently.

In ice the particles are tightly packed in fixed positions and only vibrate, so ice is hard with a fixed shape. In water the particles are close but can move past each other, so it flows and takes the container's shape. In steam the particles are far apart and move freely, filling all available space. The substance is the same; the arrangement, spacing and motion of its particles differ.
1 mark for solid versus liquid behaviour; 1 mark for gas behaviour, both explained through particle arrangement and motion.
A particle-model animation shows solid particles completely motionless and liquid particles with no attraction between them. Identify and correct both modelling errors.
Solid particles are not motionless: they vibrate about fixed positions. Liquid particles remain close and attract one another, but can move past one another; the attraction has not vanished.
1 mark for solid vibration; 1 mark for liquid attraction with mobility.

Two sealed model boxes contain the same number of particles. In A the particles are closely packed and vibrate about fixed positions; in B they are far apart and move freely. Identify the model states, compare compressibility, and explain why the particle count alone does not determine volume.

A models a solid; B models a gas. A is difficult to compress because its particles are already close together, whereas B is readily compressed by reducing the large spaces. Equal particle counts do not require equal volumes because the spacing and arrangement differ.
1 mark for solid/gas identification; 1 mark for the compressibility comparison using spacing; 1 mark for explaining why equal counts do not imply equal volume.
A wet pavement dries after the rain stops. Explain where the water goes, and why the pavement dries sooner on a windy day.

The water evaporates: its particles, always in motion, escape from the surface into the air as vapour. Wind carries away the vapour-rich air near the surface and brings drier air, so more water particles can leave quickly. On a still day the air near the wet surface stays humid and drying is slower. No new substance is formed, so evaporation is a physical change.
1 mark for evaporation as particles escaping into air; 1 for wind removing vapour and speeding drying; 1 for recognising it as a physical change.

title: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
subject: Science
objective: Which of these is an element?
Oxygen is made of only one kind of atom; water and salt are compounds and soil is a mixture.
A pure substance made of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio is called:
A compound forms when elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio, giving new properties.
Which of these is a uniform (homogeneous) mixture?
A fully dissolved salt solution looks the same throughout, so it is a uniform mixture.
Iron filings mixed with sulfur powder (not heated) can be separated with a magnet because:
each component keeps its own properties in a mixture
In a mixture the components are not chemically combined, so each keeps its own properties, including iron's magnetism.
In a teacher-led laboratory demonstration, iron and sulfur react on heating to form a black solid. What is the main product?
Heating makes iron and sulfur react chemically to form the compound iron sulfide, a new substance with new properties.
Which of these is a compound?
Carbon dioxide is carbon and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio; the others are mixtures.
Brass, made by mixing copper and zinc uniformly, is best classified as:
an alloy, which is a uniform mixture
Brass is an alloy: the metals are mixed, not chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
The smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction is:
An atom is the smallest unit of an element that participates in chemical reactions.
In water, hydrogen and oxygen are always combined in the same fixed ratio. This shows that water is:
A fixed ratio of chemically combined elements is the defining feature of a compound.
A mixture of sand and salt can best be separated by:
it cannot be separated at all
dissolving the salt in water, filtering, then evaporating the water
Salt dissolves but sand does not, so filtration removes the sand and evaporation recovers the salt.
subjective: Classify seawater as an element, compound or mixture, and justify your answer.

Seawater is a (mostly uniform) mixture. It contains water, dissolved salts and gases that are not chemically combined, keep their own properties, and can be separated by physical methods such as evaporation.
1 mark for mixture; 1 for the justification (components not chemically combined, separable by physical methods).
Explain why air is called a mixture but water is called a compound.

In air, the gases are physically mixed: their proportions can vary and each gas keeps its own properties. In water, hydrogen and oxygen are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, and water has completely different properties from both gases.
1 mark for air's variable physical mixing; 1 for water's fixed chemical combination and new properties.

Two cards describe powders. Card P: a magnet removes one component and leaves another behind. Card Q: every particle is a chemically joined unit containing two kinds of atom. Which card describes a mixture, and which a compound? Explain.
P is a mixture: physical separation shows that a component retains its properties. Q is a compound: different elements are chemically combined in each unit.
1 mark for P with physical-separation reasoning; 1 mark for Q with chemical-combination reasoning.
Classify each of the following as an element, a compound or a mixture: copper, ammonia, milk, helium, vinegar, ethanol.
Elements: copper, helium. Compounds: ammonia, ethanol. Mixtures: milk, vinegar.
1 mark for both elements correct; 1 for both compounds correct; 1 for both mixtures correct.

A display labels a uniform copper-zinc alloy as an element because it looks like one substance. Identify the error. Explain why being uniform does not by itself prove that a material is an element, and give a different kind of uniform material.

An alloy can contain more than one element even though it looks uniform. Brass contains copper and zinc, so it is a mixture, not an element. Uniformity describes the distribution of components, not the number of kinds of atom. A fully dissolved salt solution is another uniform mixture; a pure compound such as water is also an acceptable uniform example.
1 mark for rejecting the element label using copper and zinc; 1 mark for distinguishing uniform appearance from elemental composition; 1 mark for a valid further example.

title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
subject: Science
objective: In a glass of salt water, the salt is the:
The substance that dissolves is the solute; water is the solvent.
Which of these dissolves in water to form a solution?
Sugar is soluble in water; chalk, sand and oil are not.
A solution in which no more solute can dissolve at that temperature is called:
A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of solute possible at that temperature.
For most solid solutes, raising the temperature of the water generally:
turns the solute into a gas
Most solids dissolve more in hotter water, so solubility usually increases with temperature.
Stirring helps sugar dissolve faster in water mainly because it:
changes sugar into a new substance
brings fresh solvent into contact with the solute
Stirring continuously brings unsaturated solvent into contact with undissolved solute, speeding up dissolving.
An object has a mass of 100 g and a volume of 50 cm³. Its density is:
Two liquids are not mixed in this question. Equal 50 mL samples have masses 60 g and 45 g. Which sample has the greater density?
Density cannot be compared without their colours
For equal volumes, the sample with the larger mass has the larger density: 60/50 = 1.2 g/mL, compared with 45/50 = 0.9 g/mL.
A small stone sinks in a bucket of water, but a much heavier block of ice floats. What does this show?
water pushes only cold objects up
ice is less dense than water while the stone is denser
Floating and sinking depend on density, not mass alone: ice is less dense than water and the stone is denser.
Which of these is NOT a true solution?
Muddy water has solid particles suspended, not dissolved, so it is not a true solution.
A fixed mass of water is heated and expands. Its density:
The same mass now occupies a larger volume, so density = mass ÷ volume decreases.
subjective: Define solute and solvent. Identify them when a little sugar and salt dissolve completely in a glass of water.
A solute is a substance that dissolves; the solvent is the substance in which it dissolves. Sugar and salt are the solutes here, and water is the solvent.
1 mark for both definitions; 1 mark for identifying sugar/salt as solutes and water as solvent.
A sugar solution is saturated at room temperature. What does saturated mean, and how could more sugar be dissolved without adding water?
At that temperature the solution contains the maximum sugar that can dissolve. Warming it usually increases the solubility of sugar, so more sugar can dissolve.
1 mark for the temperature-qualified definition; 1 mark for warming the sugar solution.
Equal masses of sugar with the same grain size are put into equal volumes of water, one cold and one warm. Both are stirred equally. Where should sugar dissolve faster, and why?

Sugar should dissolve faster in the warm water. Higher temperature increases particle motion and generally increases the rate at which sugar dissolves. The water volumes, sugar mass, grain size and stirring are held the same for a fair comparison.
1 mark for warm water; 1 mark for explaining the temperature effect on dissolving rate.
A laboratory needs 80 cm3 of a liquid with density 1.25 g/cm3. An empty measuring vessel has mass 30 g. What total mass should the filled vessel have? Explain how you account for the vessel.
Liquid mass = density x volume = 1.25 x80 = 100 g. The balance includes the 30 g vessel, so the filled vessel should have mass 130 g.
1 mark for mass = density x volume; 1 mark for 100 g of liquid; 1 mark for adding the 30 g vessel to obtain 130 g.

Two covered cups each contain 100 mL of water at the same temperature. Cup A contains 10 g dissolved sugar; cup B contains 20 g dissolved sugar. Both can still dissolve more. A student says cup B is saturated because it is sweeter. Evaluate the claim, then describe a fair way to check saturation without tasting.

The claim is unsupported: B is more concentrated than A, but both are stated to be unsaturated. Saturation means no more solute dissolves at that temperature, not merely that the solution is sweet. Add a small measured amount of sugar, stir and allow enough time at constant temperature. Sugar remaining undissolved after mixing indicates saturation under those conditions. Never taste laboratory samples.
1 mark for distinguishing concentration from saturation; 1 mark for constant-temperature addition/stirring; 1 mark for interpreting persistent undissolved sugar after sufficient time.

title: Keeping Time with the Skies
subject: Science
objective: The length of a day is based on which repeating motion?
The Sun's movement around the galaxy
One rotation of Earth on its axis gives the cycle of day and night.
We can see the Moon because:
it is lit by Earth's city lights
The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight; we see only the sunlit part facing us.
The phases of the Moon are caused by:
the changing relative positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon
clouds covering parts of the Moon
Earth's shadow falling on the Moon
As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different portions of its sunlit half. Earth's shadow causes eclipses, not the regular phases.
One complete cycle of the Moon's phases, from full Moon to the next full Moon, takes about:
The Moon's phase cycle is about 29.5 days, which is the basis of the month.
The length of a year is based on:
One revolution of Earth around the Sun takes about 365.25 days, defining the year.
calendars were invented on a leap day
a year is about 365 and a quarter days
The extra quarter day each year adds up, so an extra day is added roughly every four years.
Luni-solar calendars add an extra (intercalary) month from time to time in order to:
keep lunar months aligned with the seasons
Twelve lunar months fall about 11 days short of the solar year, so an intercalary month realigns festivals with seasons.
On a particular night the Moon is highest in the sky around midnight. Its phase is most likely:
A full Moon is opposite the Sun, so it rises near sunset, is highest around midnight and sets near sunrise.
Ravi says, 'The Moon can only be seen at night.' His statement is:
false, because the Moon makes its own light in the day
true, because the Moon orbits only at night
true, because sunlight hides the Moon
false, because the Moon is often visible during the day too
Depending on its phase, the Moon is above the horizon during many daytime hours and can often be seen in daylight.
Days, lunar months and solar years are useful natural measures of time because they are based on:
sky motions that repeat in a predictable way
Days, months and years follow the predictable, repeating motions of the Earth, Moon and Sun.
subjective: Explain why the Moon shows phases. Make clear why Earth's shadow is not the cause of the regular phases.

The Moon is lit by the Sun on one half. As it orbits Earth, we see different portions of that lit half, producing the cycle of phases. Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which is occasional and brief, not the regular monthly cycle.
1 mark for changing view of the sunlit half as the Moon orbits; 1 for distinguishing eclipses from the regular phases.

A fictional lunar calendar uses 12 months of 29.5 days each. Calculate its year length and the difference from a 365.25-day solar year. Why might a calendar intended to follow both lunar months and seasons need an adjustment?

12 x29.5 = 354 days. The difference is 365.25-354 = 11.25 days. Without adjustment, the lunar months shift relative to the seasons; occasional extra months can help a luni-solar calendar realign them. These are approximate model values.
1 mark for 354 days and 11.25-day difference; 1 mark for the seasonal-alignment explanation.

A toy Earth completes one rotation every 8 seconds and one circuit of its lamp-Sun every 96 seconds. How many toy days fit in one toy year? Which two different motions do your calculation and labels represent?

96/8 = 12 toy days per toy year. Rotation on the axis represents the day; the circuit around the lamp represents revolution around the Sun and the year. The toy rates are not the actual rates of Earth.
1 mark for 12; 1 mark for correctly distinguishing rotation/day and revolution/year.

An observation log records a thin crescent, then a half-lit Moon, then a gibbous Moon on successively later evenings. Identify whether the visible illuminated fraction is increasing or decreasing, name this part of the cycle, and predict the next main phase if the trend continues.

The visible illuminated fraction is increasing. This is the waxing part of the cycle. After waxing gibbous, the next main phase is full Moon. The Sun continues to illuminate about half the Moon; our view of that half changes.
1 mark for increasing visible lit fraction; 1 mark for waxing; 1 mark for full Moon next.

In an approximate model, each year has 365.25 days. A calendar designer proposes 365-day years for three years, followed by one 366-day year. Compare the total calendar days with the model over four years. Explain what this corrects and why it is still an approximation.

The calendar has 3 x365+366 = 1461 days. The model has 4 x365.25 = 1461 days, so the totals match over four years. The extra day compensates for the accumulated quarter-days. A real solar year is not exactly 365.25 days, so real calendars need more detailed long-term rules.
1 mark for 1461 calendar days; 1 mark for 1461 model days; 1 mark for explaining the quarter-day correction and approximate year length.

title: How Nature Works in Harmony
subject: Science
objective: All the members of one kind of organism living in an area together form:
A population is all the individuals of one species in an area.
A community of living organisms together with the non-living surroundings forms:
An ecosystem includes both the living community and the non-living (abiotic) environment.
In most ecosystems, the producers are:
Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis, producing food for the rest of the ecosystem.
The main role of decomposers such as bacteria and fungi is to:
break down dead matter and recycle nutrients
Decomposers break down dead organisms and waste, returning nutrients to the soil for producers to use.
A food-web diagram shows both small fish and insects being eaten by a bird. What is the best reason to draw both feeding links?
The bird may use more than one food source
Energy flows only from birds to plants
All organisms occupy the same feeding level
A food web shows alternative and interconnected feeding relationships rather than one single route.
Which of these is a non-living (abiotic) component of an ecosystem?
Sunlight is a non-living component; the others are living organisms.
A coastal district plants mangroves along its shore to reduce damage from storm surges. This works mainly because mangroves:
have dense roots and trunks that act as a barrier slowing incoming waves
attract rain clouds away from the coast
release oxygen that cools the sea
make the soil salty so waves avoid it
Dense mangrove trees and roots slow and break up incoming waves, shielding the land behind them.
A food web is best described as:
a single straight chain of eating
In nature most organisms eat and are eaten by more than one species, linking food chains into a web.
A compost heap becomes very dry. Leaf breakdown slows, although microbes are still present. Which conclusion is best supported?
Abiotic conditions can affect decomposer activity
Water availability is a non-living condition that can affect the activity of decomposers. Slow breakdown alone does not prove they have vanished.
Which of these is a human-made ecosystem?
A farm field is created and maintained by people, with chosen crops replacing natural vegetation.
subjective: A grower removes all fallen leaves from one garden bed but returns well-decomposed leaf compost to another. Explain why the second practice can help nutrient recycling, and identify the group that made the compost.

Bacteria, fungi and other decomposer organisms break down the leaves. Returning decomposed material helps return mineral nutrients to the soil, where plants can use them again. This does not mean compost guarantees every nutrient a plant needs.
1 mark for decomposers; 1 mark for the dead-material-to-soil-to-plant nutrient link.
What is the difference between a population and a community? Give one example of each.

A population is all the individuals of one species in an area, for example all the neem trees in a park. A community is all the different populations of organisms living together in that area, for example the park's trees, birds, insects, fungi and grass together.
1 mark for correct definitions; 1 for a valid example of each.

A coastal planning team lists two benefits of a mangrove belt: shelter for young fish and reduced wave energy near the shore. Explain why one belt can supply both benefits without claiming that it stops every storm.

The roots and shallow sheltered water provide habitat for young fish. Dense vegetation and roots can dissipate some wave energy. Protection depends on storm strength, water depth and the belt, so mangroves do not guarantee that flooding or damage is prevented.
1 mark for the habitat explanation; 1 mark for wave-energy reduction with a sensible limit.

A bird eats both seed-eating insects and fruit. The insects feed on plants. Write two food chains ending with the bird, explain why together they form part of a food web, and state why one missing food source need not make the bird disappear immediately.

Chains: plants ->insects ->bird, and fruit-producing plants ->bird. They are linked through the bird and plants, so they are part of a food web. The bird has an alternative food source; its response also depends on food availability and other conditions.
1 mark for both valid chains; 1 mark for explaining their shared links; 1 mark for the alternative-food explanation.

In a school plot, bean plants grow beside flowering herbs. Bees visit the herbs and bean flowers. A plan would replace every plant with one crop and spray a broad insecticide. Identify two possible ecological costs and propose one lower-impact alternative.

Replacing the mixed planting can reduce habitat and food variety. A broad insecticide can kill pollinators as well as pests, which may affect pollination. An alternative is to retain flowering strips and use targeted pest management, or another justified measure that reduces non-target harm.
1 mark for loss of plant/habitat variety; 1 mark for a pollinator or other non-target effect; 1 mark for a justified lower-impact alternative.

title: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
subject: Science
objective: Two imaginary worlds have the same distance from their star, but one has no substantial atmosphere. Which conclusion is sound?
The airless world must have breathable air
Atmosphere also affects temperature and surface water conditions
Distance alone guarantees identical surface conditions
Both worlds must have identical living organisms
Distance from a star is only one condition: atmospheric composition and pressure also matter.
Earth's magnetic field helps protect life by:
deflecting many harmful charged particles coming from the Sun
The magnetic field deflects much of the solar wind, shielding the atmosphere and living things.
A field survey lists rock types, soil types, bird species and plant species. Which pair belongs in its geodiversity record?
Plant species and soil types only
Bird species and rock types only
Geodiversity concerns non-living natural variety; birds and plants are biodiversity.
If Earth had no atmosphere, its surface temperature would most likely:
swing between very hot days and very cold nights
The atmosphere traps and distributes heat; without it, temperatures would swing to extremes like on the Moon.
Which gas do green plants take in for photosynthesis?
Plants use carbon dioxide, water and sunlight to make food, releasing oxygen.
Liquid water can exist steadily on Earth's surface mainly because:
the Moon pulls the water into place
Earth's distance from the Sun and its atmosphere keep temperatures in a suitable range
Earth's distance from the Sun, combined with its atmosphere and pressure, keeps much of its water liquid.
The Moon has almost no atmosphere even though it is rocky like Earth. The main reason is:
Its weaker gravity makes it easier for gases to escape
it is too close to the Sun
The Moon has much less mass than Earth. Its low escape speed and exposure to the solar wind make retaining a thick long-lived atmosphere difficult.
the variety of living organisms in a region
the number of rocks in a region
Biodiversity is the variety of life - different species, their genes and the ecosystems they form.
Cutting down a large forest patch for roads is most likely to cause:
loss of habitats and reduced local biodiversity
more rainfall and a cooler local climate
Removing forest destroys habitats, reduces biodiversity and can warm and dry the local climate.
Which of these is an example of vegetative propagation?
A tadpole hatching from frog eggs
A mustard plant growing from a seed
A new potato plant sprouting from a potato piece with an 'eye'
A chick hatching from an egg
Vegetative propagation is new plants growing from plant parts such as stems, roots or leaves - a potato tuber piece, for instance.
subjective: A poster says: a planet at the right distance from its star must support humans outdoors. Give two reasons that the distance alone cannot justify this conclusion.

The planet might lack breathable air at suitable pressure. It might also lack accessible liquid water or suitable temperature regulation; distance alone does not determine its atmosphere, pressure or water. Radiation shielding or other clearly explained life-support needs are also acceptable.
1 mark for each of two distinct explained conditions beyond distance.

Sort these roles between the atmosphere and the magnetic field: supplying oxygen for human respiration, and deflecting many charged particles from the Sun. Why should the two protective systems not be treated as identical?

Oxygen is supplied by the atmosphere. The magnetic field deflects many solar charged particles. Air is matter surrounding Earth, whereas a magnetic field is not breathable matter; they have different functions even though both help protect the planet.
1 mark for correctly assigning both roles; 1 mark for a clear distinction between the two systems.

A nursery grows one set of plants from stem cuttings and another set from seeds formed by pollination and fertilisation. Which method is vegetative propagation? Which involves sexual reproduction? Give one reason for each.

The stem-cutting method is vegetative propagation because a new plant grows from a vegetative part of the parent. Seeds formed after fertilisation involve sexual reproduction because male and female reproductive cells fuse.
1 mark for cutting/vegetative with reason; 1 mark for fertilised-seed/sexual with reason.

An Earth-system chart shows plants releasing water vapour, clouds forming, and rain soaking into soil. Name the living, air, water and solid-Earth systems involved, then explain one link between them.

Plants belong to the biosphere; air to the atmosphere; water in rain, soil moisture and vapour participates in the hydrosphere; soil and rock belong to the geosphere. For example, plants move water from soil into the atmosphere by transpiration, and rainfall returns water to the ground.
1 mark for biosphere and atmosphere correctly identified; 1 mark for hydrosphere and geosphere correctly identified; 1 mark for a valid explained link.

A city plan protects an existing wetland, reduces burning of fossil fuels and prevents untreated sewage entering streams. Match each action to one of these problems: biodiversity loss, climate change and pollution. Explain one connection between any two problems.

Wetland protection helps limit biodiversity loss. Reducing fossil-fuel burning helps limit greenhouse-gas emissions and climate change. Sewage treatment reduces water pollution. Connections include polluted water harming species, or climate change altering habitats and biodiversity. One action can benefit more than one problem.
1 mark for the three main matches; 1 mark for one scientifically valid connection; 1 mark for explaining how that connection affects living things or their habitat.
